title: Low-latency FPGA-based electronic control system for fast preparation of defect-free atom arrays
authors: Ya-Dong Hu, Dong-Qi Ma, Tian-Yang Zhang, Liang Chen, Yi-Chen Zhang, Xiao-Kang Zhong, Wen-Yi Zhu, Hong-Jie Fan, Qing-Xuan Jie, Yan-Lei Zhang, Gang Li, Xi-Feng Ren, Xu-Liang Zhang, Guang-Can Guo, Zhu-Bo Wang, Chang-Ling Zou
abstract: The scalability of neutral atom quantum computing demands integrated electronic control systems with low latency, modular architecture, and real-time feedback capability. Here, we present an FPGA-based electronic control system that eliminates the PC from the feedback loop, integrating photon counting, real-time decision-making, and waveform generation within a unified PXIe architecture. The system achieves a total feedback latency of $282\,\mathrm{μs}$ and is validated in practical experiments by assembling defect-free atom arrays from 24 stochastically loaded optical tweezers. A single-round rearrangement achieves a filling fraction of $\sim96\%$, while feedback-controlled iterative rearrangement over five rounds boosts the success probability for generating a 10-atom defect-free array from $65.7\%$ to $95.4\%$. This system establishes the electronic infrastructure necessary for mid-circuit measurement and real-time quantum error correction on neutral-atom platforms.
summary: The paper introduces an FPGA-based electronic control system designed to overcome the slow data processing bottlenecks in large-scale neutral atom quantum computing experiments. By integrating all necessary functions onto a PXIe architecture, they achieved microsecond-level feedback latency. This breakthrough enables high-fidelity, iterative rearrangement protocols essential for building complex, defect-free quantum registers.
main_problem: The scalability of neutral atom quantum computing requires integrated electronic control systems with low latency, modular architecture, and real-time feedback capability.
main_result: The developed FPGA-based system achieves a total feedback latency of $282\,\mathrm{\mu s}$ and successfully boosts the success probability for generating a 10-atom defect-free array from $65.7\%$ to $95.4\%$.
method: The authors designed and implemented an FPGA-based electronic control system that integrates photon counting, real-time decision-making, and waveform generation into a unified PXIe architecture, eliminating the slow PC bottleneck.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a 1D array of neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezers. The system uses fluorescence detection via Optical Channel Mapping (OCM) to Single Photon Detectors (SPDs) for real-time state readout and feedback control.
key_observables: Total feedback latency ($282\,\mathrm{\mu s}$), single-round filling fraction ($\sim 96\%$), success probability of defect-free array assembly ($95.4\%$ after five rounds).
important_parameters: Trap spacing ($4.5\,\mathrm{\mu m}$), trap depth ($\sim 0.8\,\mathrm{mK}$), state preparation/gate timescales ($\sim 1-2\,\mathrm{\mu s}$).
main_assumptions: The primary bottleneck addressed is the latency of external PC control loops; the remaining single-round limit is set by atomic physics, not electronics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup detailing the optical path and electronic feedback loop components (AOD, SPDs, FPGA cards). Timing sequences show the total electronic latency, and histograms/plots demonstrate success probability improvements through iterative rearrangement protocols.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of low-latency control for fault tolerance, presents the integrated FPGA architecture, characterizes the timing overheads of each subsystem (readout, calculation, transmission), and validates the system by demonstrating high-fidelity, multi-round assembly of defect-free atom arrays.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck—the control electronics—for scaling neutral atom quantum processors. The low latency achieved is crucial for implementing mid-circuit measurement and real-time Quantum Error Correction (QEC) protocols.

Figure 3(b) presents the results of rearranging atoms from a randomly loaded array of 24 optical tweezers into a target zone of N = 10 atoms. Following the 150ms MOT load- ing step, single atoms are stochastically loaded into the 24 tweezers, giving an initial single-atom filling fraction of ap- proximately 0.6 in the target region (blue bars). After rear- rangement, the single-site filling fraction increases to approxi- mately 0.96 (red bars), substantially enhancing the probability of generating defect-free arrays; this confirms that, in neutral- atom systems, rearrangement substantially mitigates the limi- tations imposed by stochastic loading.
